entries.topic: Muscadet: Melon alone only in the three named zones
entries.claim: The Loire record calls Melon de Bourgogne Muscadet's only grape and says Muscadet is Melon de Bourgogne alone, and the Régionale question i-r0p7056l says Melon has been the sole grape of Muscadet ever since the winter of 1709.
entries.finding: The specification of the plain Muscadet AOC names Melon B as principal grape and Chardonnay B as an accessory grape, at no more than 10 per cent of a holding's plantings. INAO's standing committee took up the change in 2017, it went to national opposition in November 2018, it stands in the specification homologated by the arrêté of 5 February 2021 (amended 27 May 2021), and the arrêté of 26 November 2025 (JORF of 3 December 2025) keeps it. Muscadet Sèvre et Maine, Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire and Muscadet Côtes de Grandlieu remain Melon B alone. The history in the question stands: the specification's link to origin says the hard winter of 1709 destroyed most of the Nantes vineyard and Melon, which bears frost better, was replanted, and InterLoire says the same.

refuter.note: Searched for a stricter or newer text: the regional Muscadet rule names melon B as principal and chardonnay B as accessory at no more than 10 per cent of the holding's plantings, in the specification of 2021 and in the version adopted by the national committee on 12 June 2025; the named zones' texts (Coteaux de la Loire, Cotes de Grandlieu) read melon B alone, and a secondary page reads the same for all three. A 2024 committee paper speaks of a request to lift the accessory share to 20 per cent for a time; whether it was granted was not found, and the new texts give no figure, so they hold either way. The three old strings occur once each, in the Loire record's Melon row, r-hksiq6zd's explanation and i-r0p7056l's explanation in r1_loire.py; the stem, answer and options of both questions stay right (Melon de Bourgogne). One correction: i-r0p7056l's new text named Sevre et Maine alone, which leaves a reader to wonder about Coteaux de la Loire and Cotes de Grandlieu; it now says the other two named zones, the phrase the same bank uses in its Sevre et Maine question. ASCII kept, as r1_loire.py is. Completeness: no other line in js/, the region fragments, the CMS banks, rewrite/categories or the grape fragments calls Melon Muscadet's only or sole grape (the Melon grape fragment already says the rule loosened; MASTER m-zf6jp55w says replanted almost to the exclusion of everything else, true of 1709). The CP127 dossier and the Legifrance id were not opened from here.

entries.claim: The CMS Loire question e-ddtr2ora says the Melon variety came from Burgundy after the hard winter of 1709.
entries.finding: Melon was already in the Pays Nantais before 1709: the Muscadet specification puts the first written traces of plantings under the name Muscadet in the middle of the seventeenth century (a lease of 1635 kept at Gorges), and after the winter of 1709 Melon was replanted across the vineyard. The frost made it the grape of the region; it did not bring it.

entries.why: The frost of 1709 spread the grape across the Pays Nantais; the grape itself was there before it, so the explanation should not date its arrival to 1709.

refuter.note: Tested whether Melon arrived only after 1709. Search summaries of the Muscadet Sevre et Maine specification put the first written record of the Burgundian plant under the name Muscadet in the middle of the seventeenth century (a lease of 1635 at Gorges) and say melon B was established in the Nantes vineyard well before the frost; one secondary source puts Melon at Nantes as early as 1616. All agree the winter of 1709 is what made it the grape of the whole vineyard. So came from Burgundy after the hard winter of 1709 misdates the arrival, and the new text (came from Burgundy and took over the Pays Nantais after it) is right. The old string occurs once, in e-ddtr2ora's explanation; the answer Melon B and the other three rationales stay true. The stem of i-r0p7056l (growers replanted with a Burgundian white) speaks of the replanting, not the arrival, and L1-10 rightly leaves it. No other place dates the arrival to 1709.

entries.topic: Rueda: one white category since 2019, the main grapes at 75 per cent since 2024
entries.claim: The Rueda and Toro record teaches Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon as label categories at 85 per cent of their grape and plain Rueda as at least 50 per cent Verdejo, with Viura merely permitted in that blend; the Spain module question c-lalvjliu and the Verdejo grape fragment repeat the half.
entries.finding: The Consejo Regulador merged Rueda Verdejo, Rueda Sauvignon and Rueda into one white category, Rueda, from the 2019 vintage; the amended pliego (published nationally on 29 October 2019, in force at EU level from 3 March 2020) asked at least 50 per cent of the main whites, then Verdejo and Sauvignon Blanc, and admitted Chardonnay and Viognier as secondary. From 30 August 2024 (BOCYL of that day; EU communication of 12 June 2025) a Rueda white needs at least 75 per cent from the main whites, now Verdejo, Sauvignon Blanc, Viura, Chardonnay and Viognier, and may be all of them. A grape named on the label must still make at least 85 per cent, by EU rule. Plain Rueda therefore has no Verdejo floor of its own. The wines notes for Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon and the Verdejo label line say at least 85 per cent of a named grape, which is still true, and are left.

entries.why: Two revisions of the pliego (2019 to 2020 and August 2024) replaced the varietal categories and the half Verdejo rule; the stem of r-zd9qzdui now has two right options, Sauvignon Blanc and Chardonnay, so it is reworded to the old category and keeps its pinned id, its answer, options and accept list.

refuter.note: Tried to refute on four points. One: the merge of the varietal categories from the 2019 vintage stands on the council's note of November 2019 and on the ministry's text of the request (Sauvignon Blanc made a main variety, Chardonnay and Viognier admitted as secondary, Gran Vino de Rueda new). Two: the August 2024 change stands on the council's own press note (75 per cent main, at most 25 secondary, a wine may be all main varieties; Viura, Viognier and Chardonnay made main) and on the EU notice C/2025/3217 (from at least 50 to at least 75 per cent). Three: Palomino is still permitted, as a secondary white, on the council's variety page and in the Decanter report it hosts, so the new texts may name it in the remainder; Godello's entry as a secondary was suspended on 28 October 2024 and no new text names it. Four: the stem of r-zd9qzdui is wrong today, since Chardonnay, now a main white, may be named at 85 per cent beside Sauvignon Blanc, while Garnacha Blanca and Godello, secondary, cannot reach 85 per cent under the 75 per cent rule; the reworded stem has one right option, Sauvignon Blanc, and its id stays pinned. Corrections to the new texts: a share of three quarters is a floor, so r-99qkjr18, c-lalvjliu and the Verdejo grape question now say at least three quarters; the remainder may be any permitted white, main ones included, so the texts that said the rest from Palomino or the balance from the other whites now say the rest open to, may take or may make up; the trap's elided verb is restored (has no set share). Every old string occurs once in its file and sits in the record and path named. r-99qkjr18 still answers 85 per cent (its 75 per cent option is now explained by the text rather than made right by it), c-lalvjliu still answers at least eighty five per cent, and the Verdejo grape question still answers at least 85 per cent. Completeness: no other place in js/, the fragments, the CMS banks or rewrite/categories states the half Verdejo rule; the 85 per cent lines L1-09 leaves are true of a label naming the grape. r-99qkjr18 is held to the 60 word cap of a region question (60 words, at the cap; check-fragment passes on a copy with every spain.1 edit applied).

entries.topic: Verdejo and Verdelho: a different grape, not unrelated
entries.claim: The Rueda trap says Verdejo is not Verdelho and that the Madeira grape is unrelated.
entries.finding: They are different varieties, but not shown unrelated: the institutes' catalogue makes Verdejo a probable cross of Savagnin and Castellana Blanca on genetic analyses at Montpellier, and a DNA study of 2018 makes Verdelho an offspring of Savagnin with an unknown other parent, which would make the two half siblings. Both results rest on small marker sets, so the safe wording is a different grape, as the Verdejo and Godello grape fragments already say.

refuter.note: Looked for proof that the two are unrelated and found the reverse: the catalogue of the French institutes gives Verdejo as a probable Savagnin and Castellana Blanca cross, and two independent pages give Verdelho as an offspring of Savagnin (one a glossary on DNA of 2018, one a wine reference that lists Verdelho among Savagnin's close relations). Both rest on few markers, so a different grape is the claim true on every reading. The old string occurs once, in the Rueda record's traps[0]; it sits beside nothing it would contradict. Completeness: the Godello and Verdejo grape fragments already read a different grape; no other record calls Verdelho unrelated to Verdejo (L1-06 takes the one other unrelated, in i-fw8igegc).

entries.topic: Savagnin: kin to Sauvignon Blanc and Petit Manseng, not only to Gewürztraminer
entries.claim: The Jura record says Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc and belongs to the Traminer family, kin to Gewürztraminer (traps[0]), and its vin jaune question calls Sauvignon Blanc a different grape despite the similar name; neither says the two are kin.
entries.finding: True as far as it goes. DNA analyses (reported from 2013) show a parent and offspring tie between Savagnin and Sauvignon Blanc, and Savagnin, recorded far earlier, is taken as the likely parent; analyses reported in 2021 give Petit Manseng as a cross of Savagnin and an unknown variety, and the Oxford Companion says Savagnin may well be its parent. DNA alone cannot say which way a parent and offspring tie runs, hence likely. The grapes[1].styles line names the Traminer family and nothing about Sauvignon Blanc, so it is left; the Savagnin grape fragment already carries the likely parent on its card.

sources.says: DNA analyses of 2021 give a presumably natural cross of an unknown variety and Savagnin Blanc.

entries.why: True as written: the trap says Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc and belongs to the Traminer family, and the vin jaune explanation calls Sauvignon Blanc a different grape; neither denies kinship, and the Savagnin grape page already carries the likely parent.

refuter.note: The kinship stands (two references each give Savagnin as a likely parent of Sauvignon Blanc and of Petit Manseng, and both hedge it), but nothing in the Jura record is wrong or out of date, and the brief says edit only what is wrong. The second sommelier's own flag reads true, and it stops short; the record could. The Traminer family is the clonal group of Savagnin, Traminer and Gewurztraminer, and Sauvignon Blanc, an offspring, is not in it, so the trap's contrast holds. Petit Manseng would also widen a trap about a name. Dropped to leave; the proposed texts are kept here should the owner want them: traps[0] Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc: it belongs to the Traminer family, kin to Gewurztraminer, and DNA makes it a likely parent of Sauvignon Blanc and of Petit Manseng. questions[0].exp Sauvignon Blanc is a different grape despite the similar name, though DNA makes Savagnin its likely parent, and Chardonnay goes into other Jura whites.

entries.topic: Roussanne row: no Marsanne in Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc
entries.claim: The Régionale Roussanne row (INTRO_GRAPES) lists its wines as White Rhône blends: Hermitage, Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc (with Marsanne).
entries.finding: The Châteauneuf-du-Pape specification (homologated by decree no. 2011-1567, as published by the appellation's own federation) lists eighteen varieties: Bourboulenc, Brun Argenté (Vaccarèse), Cinsaut, Clairette, Clairette Rose, Counoise, Grenache Blanc, Grenache Gris, Grenache, Mourvèdre, Muscardin, Picardan, Piquepoul Blanc, Gris and Noir, Roussanne, Syrah and Terret Noir. Marsanne is not among them. White Hermitage is Marsanne and Roussanne. The row's reg string, N. Rhône blanc (with Marsanne), Châteauneuf blanc, Savoie, already ties Marsanne to the northern Rhône only, so it is left; Hermitage and Savoie stay where they are.

targets.new: White Rhône blends: Hermitage (with Marsanne), Châteauneuf-du-Pape blanc

sources.says: Of the thirteen grapes the appellation speaks of, the whites are Roussanne, Clairette, Bourboulenc, Picpoul and Picardan; Marsanne is absent.

entries.why: The bracket sat on the wrong appellation: Marsanne partners Roussanne in Hermitage, and Châteauneuf-du-Pape does not permit it.

refuter.note: Searched for any Chateauneuf-du-Pape text that admits Marsanne and found none: the ministry's copy of the 2011 specification lists bourboulenc, clairette, picardan and roussanne among the permitted varieties with no marsanne in the extract returned, two trade lists of the appellation's grapes omit it, and the Codex's own Roussanne grape page already says Marsanne is not permitted there. White Hermitage is Marsanne and Roussanne. The old string occurs once, in INTRO_GRAPES' Roussanne row, wines field; the new text moves the bracket to Hermitage and changes nothing else. The row's reg string ties Marsanne to the northern Rhone and stays true. No other place puts Marsanne in Chateauneuf (Cassis's Marsanne is right and is in Provence). I could not open the researcher's two PDF links (the hosts are refused here); the sources below are the ones the searches returned.

entries.topic: Rueda label lines that still hold: 85 per cent of a named grape
entries.claim: The CMS Castilla y León question e-5d1isaa8 says a Rueda Verdejo label needs at least 85 per cent Verdejo and a Rueda Sauvignon at least 85 per cent Sauvignon Blanc; the Rueda record's labels[0] (on a Rueda Verdejo label it is at least 85 per cent) and its wines notes for Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon (at least 85 per cent of the grape) say the same.
entries.finding: Since the 2019 vintage Rueda Verdejo and Rueda Sauvignon are no longer categories, but a Rueda that names one grape on its label must still hold at least 85 per cent of it, by Article 50 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/33. Each of these lines speaks of a label that names the grape, so each is still true; none repeats the old half Verdejo rule, which L1-04 corrects wherever it stands.

sources.title: Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/33, Article 50
sources.says: Where one wine grape variety is named on the label, at least 85 per cent of the product comes from it.

sources.title: Consejo Regulador de la DO Rueda, nota sobre el pliego de condiciones (November 2019)
sources.says: From the 2019 vintage the still whites are one category, Rueda, merging the old Rueda Verdejo, Rueda Sauvignon and Rueda.

entries.why: True of a label that names the grape, which is what each line describes; editing them would change wording, not facts.

refuter.note: Each line speaks of a label that names the grape, and a Rueda naming one grape must hold at least 85 per cent of it (EU rule, repeated in the pliego). e-5d1isaa8 still answers Sauvignon Blanc and its explanation is true of a Rueda labelled Verdejo or Sauvignon Blanc; labels[0] and the two wines notes likewise. None repeats the half Verdejo rule. A reader might take Rueda Verdejo for a category name, but the record's law lines (L1-04) now say the categories went in 2019, so the leave stands.

entries.topic: Muscadet lines that still hold: the grape implied, the 1709 replanting
entries.claim: The Loire record says the grape is implied by the appellation (Muscadet is Melon), its exam and trap lines match Muscadet to Melon de Bourgogne, and the stem of i-r0p7056l says a hard winter in 1709 killed most of the vineyard around Nantes and growers replanted with a hardy Burgundian white.
entries.finding: Melon B is the principal grape of every Muscadet appellation and the only grape of the three named ones; the plain appellation's accessory Chardonnay, at most 10 per cent of a holding's plantings, does not change which grape the name implies. The specification's own link to origin tells the 1709 replanting as the stem does.

sources.title: Bulletin officiel du ministère de l'Agriculture, cahier des charges de l'AOC Muscadet homologué par l'arrêté du 26 novembre 2025, publié au BO le 11 décembre 2025
sources.says: Melon B is the principal grape and chardonnay B the accessory grape of the regional Muscadet.

sources.title: INAO, cahier des charges de l'AOC Muscadet, procédure nationale d'opposition of November 2018
sources.says: After the hard winter of 1709 the vineyard was replanted with frost resistant Melon, mainly on the better sites.

entries.why: These lines are true as they stand; L1-01 corrects only the lines that call Melon the sole grape of every Muscadet.

refuter.note: Melon B is the principal grape of every Muscadet appellation and the only one of the three named zones, so the grape is implied (Muscadet is Melon), the exam line and the trap stay true, and the stem of i-r0p7056l tells the 1709 replanting as the specification's link to origin does. Nothing here calls Melon the sole grape; L1-01 takes the lines that do.

entries.topic: Navarra: Garnacha and Tempranillo neck and neck, not Tempranillo ahead
entries.claim: The Navarra record says Tempranillo has overtaken Garnacha in the plantings and is now the most planted grape (summary, the Tempranillo row, a trap, a card back and the explanation of r-fib9fgz3).
entries.finding: Tempranillo led in the denomination's register for 2022 (30.1 per cent against 27.6 for red and white Garnacha together), but the council wrote in December 2025 that Garnacha Tinta is currently the most important variety by vineyard surface, and the reports of the 2025 harvest give Garnacha Tinta 29 per cent of the vineyard and Tempranillo 26. The lead has changed hands and the two are close, so a rank either way is the volatile kind the house rules keep out.

The Navarra record's ranks were flagged in check-g12 (codexRecords) as a volatile share; read against the council and the 2025 harvest reports they are now out of date. Each old string occurs once in spain.2.json and sits in the navarra record at the path named. r-fib9fgz3 still answers Garnacha. The card front asks a rank, and its new back answers it with sources and years rather than leaving the rank unanswered; fronts are not changed by these records. entries.topic: France: Ugni Blanc the most planted white, Merlot the most planted grape
entries.claim: The France record's grape rows call Ugni Blanc the most planted white grape of France and Merlot the most planted grape in France.
entries.finding: FranceAgriMer's key figures for 2023 list Merlot at 117,369 hectares, Ugni Blanc at 106,879, Grenache at 87,862 and Chardonnay at 49,595: Ugni Blanc leads the whites by more than double, and Merlot led all grapes in 2023. Ugni Blanc gained a further 3 per cent in 2024 while Bordeaux grubbed up red vines; one trade report puts Ugni Blanc ahead of Merlot on the 2024 figures, and another, giving different 2023 hectares, implies the same turn. The 2024 varietal table itself was not read.

sources.title: FranceAgriMer, Les chiffres-cles de la filiere viti-vinicole 2023
sources.says: Principal varieties planted in 2023: Merlot 117,369 ha, Ugni Blanc 106,879, Grenache 87,862, Chardonnay 49,595.

sources.title: FranceAgriMer, Les chiffres-cles de la filiere viti-vinicole 2024 (November 2025)
sources.says: Ugni Blanc up 3 per cent on 2023; the ranking was cut off in the summary.

sources.title: Meininger, Frankreichs Reblandschaft im Wandel
sources.says: Merlot held first place for about a quarter century after Ugni Blanc led in the early 2000s; in 2023 still 103,873 ha of Merlot against 97,310 of Ugni Blanc, and Merlot down about a fifth on its five year average in the latest year.

entries.why: The Ugni Blanc line is true on every figure read; the Merlot line is true to 2023 and may have turned in 2024, which only FranceAgriMer's 2024 table can settle, so it is left and flagged.

refuter.note: Added by the second reader for completeness: check-g5 flagged the Ugni Blanc rank as volatile, and the Merlot row beside it is the one at risk. Both old lines sit in .scripts/regions/fragments/france.1.json, country.grapes[0].styles (Merlot) and country.grapes[15].styles (Ugni Blanc). If the 2024 table confirms Ugni Blanc first, the Merlot row could read One of France's two most planted grapes, true on both years' figures; no Bordeaux line changes, since Merlot leads Bordeaux on any count.
